clue.text: Wine-drinking insect, creepy-crawly

indicators.note: What you drink goes down inside you, so the wine's letters end up swallowed by the insect's.

parts.note: the crossword's standard three-letter insect, the one that lives in a hive
Asti is the sparkling white from Piedmont, and four handy letters

explanation.walkthrough: Asti and the bee are both crossword regulars: an Italian sparkler whenever wine is mentioned, a bee whenever an insect is. Learn the pair and clues like this open in seconds.
explanation.definitionFit: A beastie is the jokey word for a bug or small creature, which is exactly what a creepy-crawly is.

clue.text: Charm in a second cracking magical character up

indicators.note: cracking means breaking into, so the brief moment splits the reversed character
in a down answer, up means the word is read from the bottom, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: a rune is a letter of an old alphabet credited with magical power
a mo is a moment, informally a second

explanation.surface: A spell is broken in an instant as a magical symbol is turned upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charm' looks like a noun, a spell to go with the magic, but it is the verb meaning to delight.
explanation.definitionFit: To enamour someone is to captivate them, filling them with love, so it is to charm them.

clue.text: Express then: green light

parts.note: to express a view is to say it
'so' introduces what follows from something — and so, and then

explanation.walkthrough: The colon does the work of a link word, and both halves are such ordinary words that neither looks like fodder. 'Then' for SO is worth filing away.
explanation.definitionFit: A say-so is the permission or authority to go ahead, which is just what giving the green light grants.

clue.text: Princess seemingly enjoying orange bubble bath?

parts.note: the only way to enjoy a bath is to be in it
the orange fizzy drink: all bubbles, if not the sort you wash in

explanation.walkthrough: The picture is invented purely for the joke — a royal child sitting in a tub of orange fizz — and the question mark owns up to it.
explanation.definitionFit: An infanta is the Spanish and Portuguese title for a king's daughter who is not the heir — a princess by another name.

clue.text: Pot is as hot, thrice stirred

indicators.note: Stirring a pot mixes up whatever is in it, so these letters will not stay in the order they are given.

parts.note: four letters of fodder, exactly as they stand
h is the tap-label abbreviation for hot, and 'thrice' asks for three of them

explanation.walkthrough: What makes this look impossible is that half the fodder is spelled by an abbreviation: three separate aitches, one for each hot the clue orders.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Pot' is slang for cannabis, and hashish is the resin pressed from the same plant — one street name answering another.

clue.text: Canopy breaking, roof shearing off

indicators.note: in a down answer the roof is the top letter, and shearing off removes it

parts.note: breaking, as day breaks, means dawning

explanation.surface: A shop's canopy breaking apart in a storm, its roof torn away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' is not an anagram signal here but a synonym, as in daybreak; 'roof shearing off' drops the top letter D of DAWNING.
explanation.definitionFit: An awning is a sheet of canvas stretched on a frame over a window or shopfront, a kind of canopy.

clue.text: Short poem on a rank 14

indicators.note: In a down entry, one thing sitting on another is above it, so these letters come first.

parts.note: a haiku is the Japanese three-line poem, here minus its final letter
the clue's own A, then RATE — to rank things is to rate them

explanation.walkthrough: Hai Karate was a cheap British aftershave of the early seventies, advertised with the gag that wearing it obliged you to fend women off — hence the martial art in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: 14 is FRAGRANCE, and Hai Karate was a brand of aftershave — one particular scent standing in for the general word.

clue.text: See 27 Across
Test teams heading for Pakistan, cricket, say, talks about that

indicators.note: 'About' means round, and 'that' points back at the letter just taken — the insect closes over it.

parts.note: a cricket is one kind of insect, and 'say' marks it as an example

indicators.note: A heading sits at the top of what it names, so only the opening letter of the country is wanted.

parts.note: the opening letter of the country's name
to orate is to talk formally, at length and in public

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an England cricket tour and not one word of it means that: the teams are official bodies, and the cricket is the insect that chirps in the grass.
explanation.definitionFit: An inspectorate is an official body that examines and tests — schools, prisons, factories — so several of them really are teams that test.

clue.text: Not Old Spice!

definitions.meaning: the negative does the defining: the word wanted is the one meaning young rather than aged
the group's members took nicknames — Scary, Sporty, Ginger, Posh and one more, and it is the one more that is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is Old Spice the aftershave, which keeps the four-word clue inside the puzzle's theme. The Spice who is not the old one is Emma Bunton's Baby.
explanation.definitionFit: As a modifier the word means young or small, the opposite of old; and it is also the stage name of one of the five Spice Girls.

clue.text: Nuts cracked by trendy bankers

indicators.note: Cracking a thing opens it up, and whatever did the cracking goes into the gap it made.

parts.note: a nut for something is a fancier of it — pigeon nuts are pigeon fanciers
in = trendy, as in the in-crowd and the in thing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts cracked' is a single picture and the clue quietly splits it in two, which is why the fodder hides so well: these nuts are enthusiasts, not almonds.
explanation.definitionFit: A financier lends and invests other people's money for a living, which is the banker's trade — plural answering plural.

clue.text: Wrap up, wearing 14?

parts.note: Chanel's four-letter scent — 14 across tells you what class of thing to look for
what you have on is what you are wearing

explanation.walkthrough: Split after four letters, the answer reads as a line from a perfume counter: Coco, on. The question mark is there to carry that whimsy.
explanation.definitionFit: To cocoon someone is to wrap them up in snug layers, the way the silkworm's case encloses what is inside it.

clue.text: Underwear, inside which butt — and dangly things

indicators.note: The relative pronoun points back at the word just given, and 'inside' says the next piece goes within it.

parts.note: in Britain pants are underwear rather than trousers
the butt of a rifle or a cigarette is its blunt end

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is doing its best to embarrass you, which is exactly how a plain insertion goes unnoticed. 'Butt' is the innocent word: the end of a thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A pendant is an ornament hung from a chain so that it swings free, which makes the plural a set of things that dangle.

clue.text: Opium, say, kid smuggled into country

indicators.note: Smuggling something into a place hides it inside, which is where these letters have to go.

parts.note: the clue's country, taken whole before anything is hidden in it
to rag someone is to tease them, which is what kidding them is

explanation.walkthrough: 'Opium, say' opens a drug-smuggling story and is really the definition. This is the puzzle's key: four other clues are defined only by the number 14.
explanation.definitionFit: Opium is an Yves Saint Laurent perfume, so 'say' flags it as one example of the class the answer names.

clue.text: Dark art of server, visibly in pain

parts.note: a grim mood, or a grim joke, is a dark one
the tennis server's art is acing — serving balls the other player cannot touch

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dark art' wants to be read as one phrase, sorcery or a waiter's black arts, and it is two pieces from two different worlds.
explanation.definitionFit: To grimace is to screw your face up, which is how somebody in pain shows it without saying a word.

clue.text: Flower remains bathed in hours of sunlight

indicators.note: Anything bathed in a liquid is surrounded by it, so this word closes over the letters put between them.

parts.note: the hours between sunrise and sunset
'he remains calm' says no more than 'he is calm'

explanation.walkthrough: In a cryptic, 'flower' is usually a river — a thing that flows — so here the plain botanical reading is itself the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: A daisy is the small white and yellow flower of every lawn, so the general word names it by example.

clue.text: Stuck in Belfast, Irishman busy

indicators.note: Something stuck in a phrase is lodged there whole, so the letters sit together and in their given order.

parts.note: a run of five starting at the fifth letter of the city and carrying on over the comma

explanation.walkthrough: Two proper nouns side by side make good cover, because the eye takes them as a place and a person rather than as a string of letters to read across.
explanation.definitionFit: Astir means up and about, out of bed and already moving — the state of somebody busy rather than at rest.

clue.text: Pipe down, soon crossing new river

parts.note: sh! is what you say to make somebody be quiet

indicators.note: One thing crossing another cuts through the middle of it, so the letter lands inside the word.

parts.note: anon is the old word for soon — 'I will come anon'
n is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.walkthrough: A whole instruction to be quiet compresses into two letters here, and the river runs 240 miles across Ireland — the longest in either island.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shannon is Ireland's longest river, so the bare word 'river' defines it by example rather than by meaning.

clue.text: Going west, has set out — a different way?

indicators.note: To go west is British slang for coming to grief: a thing that has gone west has fallen apart, and so have these letters.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, with the sun setting in the surface

explanation.walkthrough: 'Going west' looks like a reversal instruction, and an answer that is itself a compass point makes that even more tempting. The phrase is slang for falling apart.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Way' means direction rather than route or method, and south-east is one of the compass's — the question mark admits the vagueness.

clue.text: Old still, preserve order

parts.note: to tin food is to preserve it in a sealed can
an order of animals, or of architecture, is a type of it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old still' sounds like a whisky-maker's kit rusting in a barn, and 'preserve order' reads as one phrase about policing. Both halves are disguised the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: A tintype is a Victorian photograph made straight onto a metal plate, and a still is a single photograph as against a moving picture.

clue.text: Kitchen implement: it has inspired me to gather up last bit of fondant!

indicators.note: To inspire is literally to breathe in, so what comes next is taken inside the letters already there.

parts.note: 'it' is sex appeal in the old sense, and SA is the abbreviation crosswords keep alive

indicators.note: Gathering things up is taking them into your arms, so this piece closes round what follows it.

parts.note: the setter signs this puzzle Paul, so 'me' is his name

indicators.note: The last bit of a word is its final letter, and that single letter is all this phrase hands over.

parts.note: the final letter of fondanT, the icing of the surface

explanation.walkthrough: Setters use 'me' for their own pen name, and this one has built himself into the word: two nested insertions, with the icing landing dead centre.
explanation.definitionFit: A spatula is the flat flexible blade used for scraping out bowls and turning food, which the general phrase names exactly.

clue.text: Piece noted through observations on a tangent

indicators.note: To note a thing is to spot it, and spotting it through a phrase means reading straight across the words.

parts.note: a run of six beginning on the last letter of the first word and crossing three gaps

explanation.walkthrough: A hidden word that crosses three word breaks is the hardest kind to see, and the musical surface — noted, observations — keeps your eye on meaning rather than letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonata is a composition for one or two instruments, so 'piece' is the plain musical sense of an everyday word.

clue.text: Stellenbosch country certainly not embraced by wine lover

indicators.note: An embrace closes round whatever it holds, so the drink named at the end wraps itself over the other letters.

parts.note: cava is Spain's sparkling wine
Stellenbosch is the wine town outside Cape Town, so the country is South Africa, SA
an emphatic refusal is a plain no

explanation.walkthrough: Wine is mentioned three ways in one sentence — a South African region, a Spanish sparkler, and a lover of the stuff — and the definition is the single last word.
explanation.definitionFit: Giacomo Casanova's memoirs made his name the standard word for a tireless seducer, so 'lover' is the eponym in everyday use.

clue.text: Sweet wrappers from Ouagadougou and Giza filling empty net

indicators.note: filling means the following letters go inside the emptied net
empty means remove the inside of net, leaving its first and last letters

parts.note: only its outer letters are kept

indicators.note: wrappers are the outside letters, the first and last of each place name

parts.note: its outer letters are taken
the same 'wrappers from' also governs Giza, after the link word and, so its outer letters G and A are taken too

explanation.surface: Sweet wrappers from two African cities stuffed into an empty goal net.
explanation.walkthrough: Ouagadougou is the capital of Burkina Faso and Giza an Egyptian city; 'wrappers from' takes their outside letters, OU and GA, which fill NT, the net left 'empty'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nougat is a chewy confection of sugar or honey, nuts and egg white, a sweet.

clue.text: Of Asian citizens, fifth of which live in European country

indicators.note: in places the preceding letters inside the European country

parts.note: UK is the abbreviation for the United Kingdom

indicators.note: fifth of means the fifth letter of the word it governs

parts.note: which refers back to the clue's citizens, whose fifth letter is taken
to live is to be, to exist

explanation.surface: A statistic about Asian citizens, a fifth of whom live in a European country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'which' points back to 'citizens'; 'fifth of' it is Z, and with BE it goes 'in' UK.
explanation.definitionFit: Uzbek is the adjective for Uzbekistan, a Central Asian republic, and its people.

clue.text: 14 to spray around tackle, he-man? I'm not posh, buy it!

indicators.note: to spray around, as scent is sprayed, means scatter the letters into a new order
not means the posh letter is excluded from the mix

parts.note: U is the old shorthand for upper-class, i.e. posh

explanation.surface: A cheeky advert urging a he-man to splash on scent, with Posh herself saying to buy it.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer at 14 is FRAGRANCE; Posh Spice is Victoria Beckham, who launched this scent with David. 'not posh' removes U from the fodder letters, and 'to spray around' rearranges what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Intimately Beckham was a perfume range launched by David and Victoria Beckham, so it is an example of a fragrance.

clue.text: 14, also Brut, set to be splashed all over

indicators.note: Splashing a liquid all over throws it in every direction, so the letters end up anywhere but where they started.

parts.note: eleven letters of fodder, Brut being another aftershave and so on theme

explanation.walkthrough: Brut is the Fabergé aftershave the boxer Henry Cooper sold on British television, so the fodder is made of the same stuff as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: 14 is FRAGRANCE, and Blue Stratos was a men's aftershave of the seventies — one brand answering the general word.

clue.text: As 'Curious', Britney Spears, is for presbyterians?

definitions.meaning: the quoted word is the scent the singer put her name to, which keeps the surface inside the puzzle's theme
the two names hold exactly the same thirteen letters in a different order, and the clue is asking you to name that relation

explanation.walkthrough: Britney Spears and Presbyterians are the most celebrated pair in the business, and Paul has hung his theme on it: Curious is her perfume, so the surface stays on scent.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue is an illustration of the word: shuffle one name's letters and the other appears, which is the relation being named.

clue.text: See 26
